posts.title: The last one to eat (scene story)

slides.text: Every Diwali, she was the last one to eat. This year, someone *noticed*.
6 a.m. Rangoli at the door, chai for twelve, the first batch of chakli on the stove.
By noon the house was full. Her name came from every direction.
Her feet hurt. She sat down for one minute. Then, from the living room:
She stood straight back up. She'd told herself the same thing for nine Diwalis.

bubbles.text: Don't sit. Don't complain. A good bahu doesn't get tired.

slides.text: Dinner. Everyone on the floor together, the family photo under the lights. She was still at the stove.
slides.cliff: Then her daughter walked into the kitchen.

slides.text: Her seven-year-old tugged at her hand. She had no answer.

bubbles.text: Mumma, why do you always eat alone?

slides.text: Her mother-in-law took the ladle from her hand.

bubbles.text: Tonight I'll make the puris. You sit.
For thirty-five years I ate last too. Not anymore.

slides.text: That night she ate hot puris with everyone. You are not the help in your own home. *You're allowed a seat at the table.*
Send this to the woman who always eats last.

posts.caption:
You don't have to eat last to be a good bahu. 🪔

So many of us grew up watching the women at home eat after everyone else.
Rest, a hot meal, a seat at the table: they aren't rewards. They're yours too.
This Diwali, pull up a chair for the woman still in the kitchen.

Send this to the woman who always eats last.
